QUESTIONS PRESENTED
1.  Does the National Voter Registration Act or a
federal consent decree prohibit Arizona from
requiring voter -registration applicants to produce
“satisfactory evidence” of U.S. citizenship to register
for federal elections when registering with a state
registration form or at a public assistance agency?

2. Does the National Voter Registration Act
prohibit Arizona from implementing a systematic
purge program within 90 days of a federal election?

INTRODUCTION
Congress, exercising its broad congressional
authority over federal election procedures,  enacted
the National Voter Registration Act (NVRA) to
promote voter participation and safeguard the
integrity of federal elections.   52 U.S.C.
§ 20501(b)(1)-(4).  This case involves two key
provisions of the NVRA .  The first eases registration
access.  It requires that any mail registration form for
federal elections demand “only” information that “is
necessary” to determine an applicant’s eligibility to
vote.  Id. § 20508(b)(1).  The second protects
registered eligible voters from erroneous removals
close to Election Day.  It prohibits states from
systematically purging suspected “ineligible voters”
from the voting rolls within 90 days of a federal
election.  Id. § 20507(c)(2).
This case also raises a critical question regarding
the proper procedure for seeking modification or
vacatur of a federal court order.  Federal Rule of Civil
Procedure 60(b) provides the exclusive means of doing
so.  That is true regardless of whether the order
resulted from a consent decree or otherwise.  And it is
true regardless of the specific complaints raised about
the underlying court order.
Two Arizona laws at issue in this case—House Bill
2492 and H ouse Bill 2243—are narrowly preempted
by the NVRA.  The former is also narrowly preempted
by an undisturbed consent decree.
H.B. 2492 prevents anyone who fails to submit
documentary proof of citizenship (DPOC) on Arizona’s
state registration form from voting, even in federal
elections.  The Federal Form does not have such a
requirement.  Thus, H.B. 2492 makes federal voter

2
registration turn not on any substantive criteria but
rather on whether an eligible Arizonan uses the State
Form or Federal Form to register.  While Arizona is
free to apply its DPOC requirement to state and local
elections, it cannot do so for federal elections for two
reasons.  First, there is a binding federal consent
decree prohibiting such arbitrary treatment between
registration forms that no party in this case has
sought to modify or vacate, as required by Rule 60(b).
Second, Arizona and petitioner have failed to show
DPOC is “necessary” for assessing voter eligibility.
They have likewise failed to show that a registration
form requiring DPOC for federal elections is
“equivalent” to one that does not require DPOC for
federal elections.  52 U.S.C. § 20506(a)(6)(A)(ii).
H.B. 2243 requires election officials to
systematically remove suspected noncitizens from the
voting rolls on a monthly basis.  Again, while Arizona
is free to implement H.B. 2243’s procedures most of
the time (and individualized removal procedures at
any time), the NVRA bars such systematic purges of
suspected “ineligible” voters in the 90 days before a
federal election, when erroneous removals are
notoriously difficult to correct.
To avoid these straightforward results, petitioner
seeks a bespoke exemption from Rule 60(b) whose
contours are ambiguous at best; interpret the NVRA’s
restriction on mail voter registration forms to “only”
information “necessary” to assess eligibility to
actually allow anything merely “helpful”; and hold
that the NVRA’s use of the term “ineligible voters”
somehow silently excludes noncitizens, who are
quintessentially ineligible to vote.  None of
petitioner’s arguments persuade.

3
This case is not about allowing noncitizens to
vote.  It is about ensuring the right of citizens to
vote.  Congress carefully crafted the NVRA to strike a
balance between promoting full participation in the
franchise and ensuring that only those who are
eligible to vote cast ballots.   This case is about
honoring that balance.  And it is about protecting the
finality of binding feder al court judgments.   This
Court should afford the NVRA’s terms their ordinary
meaning, respect an existing federal  court judgment
and the proper procedures for adjustments to it, and
affirm.
STATEMENT OF THE CASE
1. The NVRA “requires States to provide
simplified systems for registering to vote in federal
elections,” Young v. Fordice, 520 U.S. 273, 275 (1997),
to “increase the number of eligible citizens who
register to vote in elections for Federal office,” and to
“enhance[] the participation of eligible citizens as
voters in elections for Federal office.”  52 U.S.C.
§ 20501(b)(1)-(2).  To achieve these goals, Congress
“erected a complex superstructure of federal
regulation atop state voter -registration systems.”
Arizona v. Inter Tribal Council of Ariz., Inc., 570 U.S.
1, 5 (2013) (ITCA).
Under that complex superstructure, Section 6 of
the NVRA requires states to “accept and use the mail
voter registration application form” (Federal Form)
made available by the Election Assistance
Commission ( EAC).  52 U.S.C . § 20505(a)(1)-(2).
States can “develop and use” their own s tate-created
forms (State Forms) to register voters for federal
elections.  Id. § 20505(a)(2).  But, under Section 9 of
the NVRA, those forms  “may require only such

4
identifying information . . . and other information . . .
as is necessary to enable the appropriate State
election official to assess the eligibility of the
applicant and to administer voter registration.”  Id.
§§ 20505(a)(1)-(2), 20508(b)(1).  And Section 7
requires state voter registration agencies to distribute
either the Federal Form or “the [voter registration
agency] office’s own form if it is equivalent to the
[Federal] form.”  Id. § 20506(a)(6)(A)(ii).
The NVRA also imposes requirements for
“removing ineligible persons” from the voter rolls .
Husted v. A. Philip Randolph Inst., 584 U.S. 756, 761
(2018).  But it protects eligible voters from improper
removal by prohibiting systematic voter removal
within 90 days of a federal election.  52 U.S.C.
§ 20507(c)(2)(A) (90-Day Provision).
2. This Court has considered Arizona’s voter
registration requirements multiple times.  In ITCA,
the Court held that Arizona could not require Federal
Form applicants to submit DPOC  to register for
federal elections because Section 6 requires states to
“accept the Federal Form as a complete and sufficient
registration application” to vote for federal offices ,
and the Federal Form does not include a DPOC
requirement.  570 U.S. at 9.
In ITCA, this Court suggested that Arizona could
ask the EAC to include DPOC as a necessary item on
the Federal Form.  Id. at 19-20.  Arizona asked; the
EAC denied the request; and Arizona unsuccessfully
challenged that decision .  The court of appeals held
that Arizona had failed to show that it needed DPOC
to verify eligibility .  See Kobach v. U.S. Elec tion
Assistance Comm’n, 772 F.3d 1183, 1197-98 (10th Cir.
2014).  This Court denied certiorari.  576 U.S. 1055
(2015) (mem.).

5
After ITCA, Arizona adopted a bifurcated voter
registration system.  For those who applied using the
Federal Form without DPOC, election officials
checked the Arizona Department of Transportation
(ADOT) data available to them through the voter
registration system.  25-1017 RNC Cert. Pet.
App.475a (Pet.App.).  If that data confirmed
citizenship, the applicant became a full-ballot voter; if
not, the applicant was  registered as a federal -only
voter.  Id.  Election officials ran no similar search for
State Form applicants without DPOC.  Id.  State
Form applicants without DPOC were rejected even
when election  officials had access to their proof of
citizenship through ADOT.
The League of United Latin American Citizens of
Arizona (LULAC) and Arizona Students’ Association
(ASA) challenged this system, alleging that hinging
federal registration status solely on the paper form
used to register violated the First and Fourteenth
Amendments.  Pet. App.475a.  To resolve these
constitutional claims, then-Arizona Secretary of State
Reagan, represented by then -Attorney General
Brnovich, agreed to a c onsent decree ( LULAC
Consent Decree), dictating that Arizona election
officials would treat Federal and State Form
registrants the same.  Pet. App.484a-486a.  After the
Decree, Arizona could not deny State Form applicants
the ability to vote in federal elections only  because of
failure to submit DPOC.
3. In 2022, the Arizona legislature enacted House
Bill 2492.  See H.B. 2492, 55th Leg., 2d Reg. Sess.
(Ariz. 2022).   As relevant here, H.B. 2492 required
registrars to wholly reject State Form applications
that lacked DPOC.  A.R.S. § 16-121.01(A), (C).  Under
H.B. 2492, Arizona election officials would continue to

6
use the ADOT database to confirm the citizenship of
Federal Form applicants who did not provide DPOC
and register them as full -ballot voters if possible.
However, election officials would not do the same for
State Form applicants without DPOC, leading to the
rejection of applicants even when officials could verify
their citizenship with ADOT.
Arizona also passed Ho use Bill 2243, imposing
monthly systematic voter registration cancellation
procedures.  See H.B. 2243, 55th Leg., 2d Reg. Sess.
(Ariz. 2022); see also A.R.S.  § 16-165(A)(10), (E)-(L).
These procedures involve comparing voter
registration lists against various databases and
cancelling voters who are flagged  as potential
noncitizens in those databases.  Id.
4. R espondents challenged the new laws, filing
suit against the Arizona Secretary of State and
others.  Petitioner—and, later, the Arizona Senate
President and House  of Representatives Speaker —
intervened to defend the laws.
a. T he district court granted partial summary
judgment for respondents, holding that Arizona could
not impose H.B. 2492 on State Form  applicants for
registration for federal elections because (i) the
Decree, which had never been modified or set aside,
proscribes the conduct , and (ii)  the Requirement
violated the NVRA.  Pet. App.365a-366a.  The court
also held that H.B. 2243 violates the NVRA insofar as
“[it] allow[s] systematic cancellation of registrations
within 90 days of federal elections.”  Pet.App.357a.
At trial, r espondents established that the
databases relied upon for cancellations under
H.B. 2243 contain stale and inaccurate citizenship
information for some voters, which would cause U.S.

7
citizens to be flagged as  noncitizens and purged
within 90 days of an election .  Pet. App.203a-206a,
222a.  Respondents also established, through
unrebutted evidence, that noncitizen voting in
Arizona is exceedingly rare.  Pet.App.227a-229a.
b. Petitioner sought a partial stay on some issues
but not others —and not on the 90 -Day Provision
issue.  This Court granted the application in part .
Pet.App.426a.
c. T he Ninth Circuit affirmed in relevant part.
On H.B. 2492, the Ninth Circuit  reasoned that both
the undisturbed Decree , a s well as  the NVRA
provision limiting State Forms to information that is
“necessary” to assess eligibility , barred Arizona’s
DPOC requirement.  Pet. App.47a-52a.  It likewise
held that, as to public assistance agencies, H.B. 2492
violated the NVRA’s separate provision dictating that
“state forms supplied to public assistance agencies be
‘equivalent’ or ‘virtually identical’ to the federal form.”
Pet.App.51a (first quoting 52 U.S.C. §
20506(a)(6)(A)(ii); and then quoting Pet.App. 37a-
38a).
As for Arizona’s program of cancelling voter
registrations, the Ninth Circuit held that Arizona’s
“periodic cancellation of registrations violates t he
90-day Provision . . . to the extent that [it] authorizes
systematic cancellation of registrations within 90
days before a federal election.”  Pet.App.47a.  Judge
Bumatay dissented.  Pet.App.77a.
d. The Ninth Circuit denied rehearing en banc.
Pet.App.163a.
SUMMARY OF THE ARGUMENT
I. H.B. 2492 violates an existing federal consent
decree and both Sections 7 and 9 of the NVRA.

8
A. It is undisputed that the LULAC Consent
Decree prohibits Arizona from requiring DPOC for
State Form applicants to vote in federal
elections.  The Decree is a final and enforceable
federal court judgment.  And no party has ever sought
to vacate or modify the Decree.   That should be the
end of the matter.  Neither petitioner nor the United
States presents any compelling reason to evade the
strictures of Rule 60(b)(5) and refuse to find the
Decree enforceable on an ongoing basis  unless it is
modified or vacated.
B. H .B. 2492 also violates the NVRA.   Section 9’s
requirement that m ail registration  forms, including
State Forms, require “only” information that is
“necessary” to assess eligibility means that states can
require only essential information  for federal
registration.  H.B. 2492 does not meet that
standard.  Congress considered and rejected an
amendment to the NVRA that would have expressly
permitted states to require DPOC.   And Arizona has
failed to put forward any evidence showing that
DPOC is “necessary” to assess an applicant’ s
qualifications to vote.  The interpretations pressed by
petitioner and the United States would gut the
necessity requirement, afford states virtually
unlimited discretion to erect barriers to federal
registration, and render the NVRA toothless.
H.B. 2492 as applied at public assistance agencies
also runs afoul of Section 7  because it renders the
State and Federal Forms not “equivalent” within the
meaning of the NVRA.   An applicant who submits
federally qualifying information on the State Form
will be denied federal registration, while an
identically situated applicant who submits the exact
same information on the Federal Form will be

9
registered as a federal voter.  The two forms are thus
not equivalent by any standard.
II. Arizona’s voter purge law, H.B. 2243, violates
the NVRA’s 90-Day Provision, which prohibits states
from “systematically remov[ing]” “ineligible voters”
from the voting rolls within 90 days of a federal
election.
A. Noncitizens are “ineligible” to vote, and when
they appear on th e voting rolls, they are “ineligible
voters” within the meaning of the statute.  The NVRA
therefore prohibits programs designed to
systematically remove suspected noncitizens within
90 days of a federal election.
B. Petitioner and the United States posit that
“ineligible voters” refers only to voters who were
previously eligible to vote.   But the statute does not
say that.  And their reading cannot be squared with
the NVRA’s ordinary meaning, the statutory context,
or the core purpose of the 90-Day Provision.
C. Nor would affording the NVRA its plain
meaning somehow deny states the ability to remove
noncitizens, like all other ineligible voters, from their
registration lists.  States can remove noncitizens on
an individualized basis at any time, and they can
systematically remove such voters outside of the
90-day period.  All that the 90-Day Provision does is
protect the right of citizens to vote by avoiding
erroneous removals close to an election.
ARGUMENT
I. THE CONSENT DECREE AND THE NVRA
BAR H.B. 2492
Both a federal consent decree and the NVRA
prohibit Arizona from requiring DPOC for people

10
seeking to register to vote in federal elections using
Arizona’s State Form.
A. The LULAC Consent Decree Bars
Arizona’s Enforcement Of H.B. 2492
1. Consent Decrees Are Binding, Final
Judgments That May Be Disturbed
Only Under Rule 60(b)
Under the LULAC  Consent Decree, Arizona
election officials must  treat voter registration
applicants similarly for federal elections , whether
they use the Federal or State Form.  Pet.App.476a.
No party disputes that H.B. 2492  conflicts with the
Decree.  The only question presented is whether the
Decree continues to “prohibit Arizona from requiring
voter-registration applicants to produce ‘satisfactory
evidence’ of U.S. citizenship when registering [ for
federal elections] with a state registration form.”
Pet’r Br. i.  The Decree has been  neither vacated nor
modified under Rule 60(b), so it remains an
enforceable, binding, and final ju dgment.  Arizona
agrees.  Ariz. Resp’t Br. 21 (Ariz. Br.).  Because the
Decree continues to have binding force, the answer to
the first question presented is yes.
a. “[A] consent decree is a final judgment  . . . .”
Rufo v. Inmates of Suffolk Cnty. Jail, 502 U.S. 367,
391 (1992).  In a consent decree, the parties negotiate
an agreement that is “reflected in, and . . . enforceable
as, a judicial decree that is subject to the rules
generally applicable to other judgments. ”  Id. at 378.
And like all judicial orders, parties “are expected to
obey that decree until it is modified or reversed, even
if they have proper grounds to object to the order .”
GTE Sylvania, Inc. v. Consumers Union of U.S., Inc.,
445 U.S. 375, 386 (1980).

11
Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 60(b) dictates  the
grounds for seeking relief from a final judgment.  “On
motion and just terms, the court may relieve a
party . . . from a final judgment,” including because
“applying it prospectively is no longer equitable.”
Fed. R. Civ. P. 60(b).  Rule 6 0(b) provides the
exclusive path for “a party to seek relief from a final
judgment.”  Gonzalez v. Crosby , 545 U.S. 524, 528
(2005).  “I t is Rule 60(b)’s standard —and only Rule
60(b)’s standard —that applies when a party seeks
relief from final judgment. ”  BLOM Bank SAL v.
Honickman, 605 U.S. 204, 214 (2025).  And Rule 60(b)
applies all the same when it comes to consent decrees:
This Court has repeatedly held and reaffirmed that
Rule 60(b) provides the mechanism to  “ seek[] relief
from an injunction or consent  decree.”  Agostini v.
Felton, 521 U.S. 203, 215 (1997); see also Horne v.
Flores, 557 U.S. 433, 447 (2009); Rufo, 502 U.S. at 378
(recognizing that consent decrees are “subject to” the
“generally applicable” rules for final judgments).
These basic principles resolve the question
presented.  All agree that the Decree, if it remains

II. ARIZONA’S SYSTEMATIC REMOVAL OF
INELIGIBLE VOTERS VIOLATES THE
NVRA’S 90-DAY PROVISION
The NVRA mandates that a “State shall complete,
not later than 90 days prior to the date of a primary
or general election for Federal office, any program the
purpose of which is to systematically remove the
names of ineligible voters from the official lists of
eligible voters. ”  52 U.S.C. §  20507(c)(2)(A).
H.B. 2243’s removal program violates the NVRA
because it systematically purges voters from the
voting rolls within 90 days of a federal election.
That H.B. 2243 would “systematically remove”
individuals from the voter registration list is
undisputed.  The United States also concedes that
H.B. 2243 constitutes a “program” under the NVRA’s
90-Day Provision.  U.S. Br. 32.  To prevail, petitioner
and the United States would have this Court hold —
contrary to commonplace understanding —that
noncitizens are not “ineligible voters” by dramatically
contorting the relevant statutory text.  Under that
reading, the 90 -Day Provision would not bar “any”
program to remove ineligible voters subject to
specified exceptions but only one type of program : a
program to remove voters who moved.  To reach that

34
improbable conclusion, petitioner and the United
States ask this Court to redefine “ineligible voters” as
voters who were once eligible but are no longer.  See
U.S. Br. 33; Pet’r Br. 45-46.  That argument and
others defy the 90 -Day Provision’s text, ignore the
broader statutory context, and would subvert the
overriding purpose of protecting the right of citizens
to vote.
The NVRA means what it says: s tates are free to
engage in systematic list maintenance, just not within
90 days of a federal election.  And s tates remain free
to engage in non-systematic removals during those 90
days.  There is no reason to adopt anything other than
the plain and commonsense meaning of the text.
A. The NVRA’s 90- Day Provision Prohibits
Arizona’s Systematic Removal Program
1. As the United States concedes, the plain
meaning of the term “ineligible voter” does “[o]f course
. . . describe noncitizens.”   U.S. Br. 32.  No party
disputes that noncitizens are not permitted to vote in
federal elections, see 18 U.S.C. § 611, and noncitizens
are thus definitionally “ineligible” to vote.  See
Ineligible, Merriam -Webster’s Collegiate Dictionary
596 (10th ed. 1993) (“not qualified for
a[] . . . position”).  And a “voter” is “a person who can
or does vote.”  Voter, Collins English Dictionary 1721
(3d ed. 1994).  Because a noncitizen who has
mistakenly been registered to vote appears on a
state’s list of eligible voters , despite their legal
ineligibility, that person is an “ineligible voter.”
2. The 90 -Day Provision’s context and structure
support reading “ineligible voter” to include
noncitizens.  The statutory scheme envisions only two
categories of voters: “eligible” and “ineligible.”  It does

35
not contemplate any third category.  A noncitizen who
is on the voter rolls is not, of course, an “eligible
voter,” leaving only “ineligible voter” as a possible
descriptor.  Congress knew how to legislate  broadly
when identifying the covered activity ( “any
program”), but it chose limited, mutually exclusive
language when describing what kinds of voters there
can be (“ineligible voters” and “eligible voters”).
There is no exception  to the 90 -Day Provision for
systematic citizenship -based-removal programs.
Congress knew how to create exceptions and did so
expressly, listing several exceptions after the general
rule.  See 52 U.S.C. §  20507(c)(2)(B).  Systematic
citizenship-based-removal programs are not listed.
Because “Congress explicitly enumerate[d] certain
exceptions to a general prohibition, additional
exceptions are not to be implied . . . .”  TRW Inc., 534
U.S. at 28.
3. The neighboring sections likewise demonstrate
noncitizens are “ineligible voters” covered by the
general rule.
The 90 -Day Provision is located in 52 U.S.C.
§ 20507, and provisions in three surrounding
sections—Sections 5, 7, and 9—all refer to
“citizenship” as an “eligibility requirement,” such that
noncitizens must be ineligible voters.  See id.
§ 20504(c)(1), (c)(2)(C)(i); id.  § 20506(a)(6)(A)(i); id.
§ 20508(b)(2).  Citizenship is in fact the only  form of
“eligibility” Congress specifically mentioned.
It is the “normal presumption” that “within a
single statute, [a] term bears a consistent meaning
throughout.”  Azar v. Allina Health Servs. , 587 U.S.
566, 576 (2019).  That is particularly true when the
terms are in “close proximity,” as that is a “classic

36
case for application” of the presumption.  Comm’r v.
Lundy, 516 U.S. 235, 250 (1996) ( citation omitted ).
The NVRA’s repeated reference to citizenship as an
“eligibility requirement” creates a strong
presumption that Section 8’s similar reference to
“ineligible voters” includes voters who are ineligible
by reason of citizenship.  There is no “good reason or
evidence to unseat” that presumption.  Azar, 587 U.S.
at 576.
4. The NVRA’s broader purpose —to protect
eligible citizen voters who are at risk of erroneous
removal from the rolls —also supports applying the
90-Day Provision to systematic removals based on all
forms of purported ineligibility, not just some.
As Congress expressly concluded, “unfair
registration laws and procedures can have a direct
and damaging effect on voter participation in
elections.”  52 U.S.C. § 20501(a)(3).  Against that
backdrop, Congress recognized both the “costs” and
“benefits of systematic programs” to audit the voter
rolls.  Arcia v. Fla. Sec’y of State, 772 F.3d 1335, 1346
(11th Cir. 2014) .  While “[a]t most times during the
election cycle, the benefits of systematic programs
outweigh the costs,” “the calculus changes” in the
“final days before an election.”  Id.
That is because even well -meaning programs to
systematically remove ineligib le voters can
mistakenly remove eligible citizen voters.  Real-world
examples abound.  Arizona’s own databases identified
over 6,000 established citizens as noncitizens.  See
Pet.App.203a.  One Alabama program removed
“thousands of United States citizens” eligible to vote,
with citizens making up a majority  of the voters
removed.  See Ala. Coal. for Immigrant Just. v. Allen,
No. 2:24-cv-1254, 2024 WL 4510476, at *1 (N.D. Ala.

37
Oct. 16, 2024).  A systematic Florida program that
used the same  federal SAVE database as H.B. 2243
mistakenly removed U.S. citizens from the voting
rolls.  See Arcia, 772 F.3d at 1339-41.  And a Virginia
program likewise removed citizens from the rolls.  See
Va. Coal. for Immigrant Rts. v. Beals, 803 F. Supp. 3d
454, 461 (E.D. Va. 2025).
Last-minute systematic removals threaten the
ability of eligible voters to cast their ballots in federal
elections—and the “indelibly clear” and
“constitutionally protected right to vote” of all
citizens.  Reynolds v. Sims, 377 U.S. 533, 554 (1964).
Because eligible voters removed during the final days
before an election “will likely not be able to correct the
State’s errors in time to vote,” Arcia, 772 F.3d at 1346,
systematic programs pose too high a risk that eligible
citizen voters will be disenfranchised.  This threat
exists regardless  of whether a voter is removed
because they are inaccurately identified as a
noncitizen, as a nonresident, or as “ineligible” for
some other reason.
The 90 -Day Provision, properly read, “carefully
balance[s]” the need for “ accurate and current voter
registration rolls ” with the desire to encourage
“eligible citizens [to] register to vote.”  Id. (citation
omitted).
B. The Alternative Reading s Advanced By
Petitioner And The United States Cannot
Be Squared With The NVRA’s Text,
Context, Or Purpose
Although noncitizens are ineligible to vote,
petitioner and the United States argue the NVRA’s
reference to “ineligible voters” does not include
noncitizens.  That atextual argument does not work.

38
1. Petitioner—though notably not the United
States—advances two arguments that cannot be
squared with the text of the NVRA.
a. Petitioner first argues that “noncitizens are not
‘voters’ at all” because the plain meaning of “voter”
refers to “a person who has the qualifications entitling
him to vote.”  Pet ’r Br. 42.  This reading is
nonsensical.  The statute does not refer merely to
“voters” but instead to both “eligible voters”—those
who have the necessary qualifications to vote—and
“ineligible voters” —those without the necessary
qualifications to vote.  See, e.g. , 52 U.S.C.
§ 20507(a)(4), (c)(2)(A).  By using both terms,
Congress made clear a “voter” is a person who appears
on a “list[] of eligible voters,” id.  § 20507(c)(2)(A),
irrespective of their qualifications.
Accepting petitioner’s definition —that the term
“voter” alone accounts for a person’s eligibility to
vote—makes nonsense of the statutory terms.  It
would render the phrase “eligible voter” pure
surplusage, since every “voter” (under petitioner ’s
reading) would definitionally be eligible.  See Fischer
v. United States, 603 U.S. 480, 493 (2024) (noting the
“obligation to give meaning where possible to each
word and provision in” a statute).  And it would,
conversely, render the term “ineligible voter” an
oxymoron, since no voter could both “ha[ve] the
qualifications” fo r voting, Pet ’r Br. 42, and also be
“ineligible” to vote.  This Court presumes that “a
contradiction in terms” and “oxymoron [are] not . . .
typical feature[s] of congressional drafting.”  Stern v.
Marshall, 564 U.S. 462, 477 (2011).
b. Petitioner next argues that despite the 90-Day
Provision referencing “any program,” it applies only
to a “program” established under subsection (a)(4),

39
which requires states to conduct “a general program”
to remove ineligible voters by reason of “the death of
the registrant” or “a change in the residence of the
registrant.”  52 U.S.C. § 20507(a)(4); see Pet’r Br. 47.
That interpretation is textually foreclosed by the
90-Day Provision itself.  Under petitioner’s reading,
removals under subsection (a)(3) fall outside the 90 -
Day Provision by operation of the word “program.”
But subsection (c)(2) specifically lists—and exempts—
certain removals under subsection (a)(3).  See 52
U.S.C. §  20507(c)(2)(B)(i) (exempting removals
“described in paragraph (3)(A) or (B) . . . of subsection
(a)”).  It would make no sense for Congress to
explicitly exempt certain (a)(3) programs from the 90-
Day Provision if the 90 -Day Provision was limited to
(a)(4) “program[s]” from the start.
Petitioner’s definition also suggests that the 90 -
Day Provision says “any program” but means just one
program: removal based on change in residence.
Contra Patel v. Garland, 596 U.S. 328, 338 (2022) (“As
this Court has repeatedly explained , the word ‘any’
has an expansive meaning.”) (citation modified).  That
is because the 90 -Day Provision specifically exempts
removals based on death of the registrant —the only
other category covered by (a)(4).  52 U.S.C.
§ 20507(c)(2)(B)(i).  That too is nonsensical.  Congress
knew how to refer to subsection (a)(4) programs
specifically if it wanted to; it did so in the provision
immediately preceding the 90 -Day Provision.  Id.
§ 20507(c)(1) (explaining how a State can meet its list
maintenance obligations “of subsection (a)(4)”).
Congress’s different language in the 90 -Day
Provision and subsection (a)(4) further shows they
cover different removal programs.  Unlike subsection
(a)(4), which speaks to “a general program” for

40
removals based on death or changes in residence, the
90-Day Provision sweeps in “ any program” to
“systematically remove the names of ineligible
voters.”  Id.  § 20507(a)(4), (c)(2) (emphasis added) .
Petitioner’s reading would erase the “ usual
presumption that ‘differences in language .  . . convey
differences in meaning.’”  Ysleta Del Sur Pueblo v.
Texas, 596 U.S. 685, 698 (2022) (citation omitted).
2. The United States, for its part, advances only
one textual defense of Arizona’s statute (at 36 -37).
The theory, shared by petitioner (at 42-46), is that the
phrase “ineligible voters” means something other
than a person who is ineligible to vote— and that
Congress, without ever defining the term, meant to
refer exclusively to individuals who once  could
lawfully vote but have since lost their eligibility.
In their telling, Section 8 creates a cascading
series of complex unstated definitions.  First,
individuals seeking to register to vote are “applicants”
who are either “eligible applicants” or “ineligible
applicants.”  At this stage, petitione r and the United
States give “eligibility” and “ineligibility” their
ordinary definitions, referring, respectively, to
applicants who have the qualifications to vote and
those who do not.  Second, only “eligible applicants”
become “registrants.”  And third, “registrants” are
“eligible voters” unless they lose eligibility, in which
case they become “ineligible voters.”  Under this view,
because “ineligible voters” must have once been
“registrants,” who, in turn, must have once been
“eligible applicants,” the  90-Day Provision’s
prohibition against systematically removing
“ineligible voters” within 90 days of an election does
not cover noncitizens because they were never
“eligible applicants” to begin with.

41
Every court to consider this convoluted reading of
the statute has rejected it.  See, e.g. , Va. Coal. for
Immigrant Rts. v. Beals, No. 24 -2071, 2024 WL
4601052, at *1 (4th Cir. Oct. 27, 2024); Beals, 803 F.
Supp. 3d at 473; Allen, 2024 WL 4510476, at *1.  And
the United States itself previously rejected it as
contradicting the plain text of the statute .  See U.S.
Br. 32 n.3.   The government was right then and is
wrong now.
a. For starters, neither petitioner nor the United
States points to any dictionary definition—or, for that
matter, any other textual support—suggesting that
“ineligible,” “voter,” or “ineligible voter” describe s
only a previously eligible individual.  And the notion
that an “ineligible voter” is only someone who was
previously eligible to vote cannot be squared with
petitioner’s preferred definition of a “voter”—a person
who has  “the qualifications entitling him to vote.”
Pet’r Br. 42.  Neither that definition of voter nor any
identified definition of “ ineligible” hinges on when a
voter has or lacks the qualifications to vote.
Petitioner and the United States’ theory also
conflates “registrants” with “voters.”  According to
petitioner and the United States, “registrants” a re
people who were once eligible applicants.  U.S. Br. 34;
Pet’r Br. 44.  And, according to petitioner and the
United States, “voters” has the same meaning: people
who were once eligible applicants.  In petitioner and
the United States’ telling, the 90-Day Provision would
have the same meaning if, instead of prohibitin g
states from removing “the names of ineligible voters
from the official lists of eligible voters,” 52 U.S.C.
§ 20507(c)(2)(A), Congress instead prohibited states
from removing “the names of i neligible registrants
from the official lists of eligible voters.”  That would

42
violate the cardinal rule that courts “assume[]
different meanings were intended” “ when the
legislature uses certain language in one part of the
statute and different language in another.”  Sosa v.
Alvarez-Machain, 542 U.S. 692, 711 n.9 (2004);  see
also Beals, 2024 WL 4601052, at *2 (explaining that
petitioner’s theory requires reading the distinct terms
of “voters” and “registrant” as “having the same
meaning”).
Nothing overcomes that assumption.  There is no
statutory evidence Congress intended to equate the
two terms.  Congress never once linked “registrants”
to “voters” in the way petitioner and the United States
suggest, nor did Congress textually limit “ineligible
voters” to those who were once “registrants.”  In the
absence of any textual evidence that the NVRA
silently enacted this three- tier applicant -registrantvoter model,  the basic presumption that different
terms have different meanings should govern.  Sosa,
542 U.S. at 711 n.9.
“[E]ven supposing [this] theory were a textually
permissible way to understand the statute,” this
Court “do[es] not usually pick a conceivable -butconvoluted interpretation over the ordinary one.”
Stanley v. City of Sanford, 606 U.S. 46, 55-56 (2025);
cf. Mullin v. Doe, 609 U.S. 324, 342 (2026) (“Statutory
interpretation proceeds on the assumption that those
who draft and enact a provision generally intend its
terms to mean what they mean in ordinary usage. ”).
The NVRA’s reference to “ineligible voters” for
systematic removal most straightforwardly refers to
people whose names appear on the voting rolls , but
who are not eligible to vote.  That definition plainly
encompasses suspected noncitizens.

43
b. The reading advanced by petitioner and the
United States would also create other problems in the
statute.
For one thing, it would render nonsensical
Congress’s repeated use of the term “official lis ts of
eligible voters. ”  See 52 U.S.C. §  20507(c)(2)(A); see
also id. § 20507(a)(3), (a)(4), (b)(2), (d)(1), (d)(3), (f),
(i)(1).  The term “voters” cannot mean only those who
were once eligible, because voter registration systems
are not perfect.  No state does —or could—maintain
an “official list[]” of only voters who were once eligible.
The only “official lists” that exist—and thus the only
lists that Congress could have been describing —are
states’ lists of all persons whom the states have
deemed eligible to vote during the registration
process.  Petitioner’s contrary reading would suggest
Congress centered the 90 -Day Provision around lists
that do not and could not exist.
For another, their reading cannot be squared with
the structure of the 90 -Day Provision for the same
reason that petitioner’s “program” definition fails.
The Provision’s operative section, 52 U.S.C.
§ 20507(c)(2), exempts three specific types of
removals from the 90-Day Provision’s coverage: those
“described in paragraph (3)(A) or (B) or (4)(A) of
subsection (a).”  Those three sections describe three of
the four ways that “a registrant may . . . be removed”:
“at the request of the registrant,” “by reason of
criminal conviction or mental incapacity,” or due to
“the death of the registrant.”  Id. § 20507(a)(3), (4).  If
petitioner is correct that “ineligible voters” are
exclusively a subcategory of “registrants” —and thus
that the 90 -Day Provision covers only systematic
programs to remove registrants—then the 90 -Day
Provision covers only the narrow fourth situation not

44
mentioned in subsection (c)(2): systematic removals
premised on a “change in the residence of the
registrant.”  Id. § 20507(a)(4)(B).
It would make little sense for Congress to craft a
broad provision barring “any program the purpose of
which is to systematically remove the names of
ineligible voters,” id.  § 20507(c)(2)(A) (emphasis
added), if Congress wanted to prevent only those
removals based on changes in residence.  And
elsewhere in Section 8 , Congress provided detailed
procedures governing when and how states can
remove voters due to changes in residence.  See 52
U.S.C. §  20507(c)(1), (d).  This Court should not
“[d]raw[] meaning” from ambiguity when “Congress
has shown that it knows how to [address an issue] in
express terms.”  Samantar v. Yousuf , 560 U.S. 305,
317 (2010) (citation omitted).
The United States attempts to justify this bizarre
reading, suggesting it is explained by “the NVRA’s
protracted statutory history, which culminated . . . in
a ‘compromise.’”  U.S. Br. 40.  The United States also
suggests that structuring the 90 -Day Provision as a
separate statutory subsection makes sense because it
would accommodate Congress later “expand[ing]” the
“exceptions to the gener al-removal ban” through
statutory amendments.  Id. at 40- 41.  Neither
justification is persuasive.
First, the United States is wrong about the
legislative history, which described the 90 -Day
Provision in broad terms.   As the House conference
report put i t, the NVRA “does not permit a State to
conduct a systematic procedure to confirm voting lists
within 90 days before a Federal election.”  H.R. Rep.
No. 103 -66, at 20  (emphasis added).  The House
committee report likewise stated that the 90 -Day

45
Provision covers “any program,” including “a mailing
or a door to door canvas.”  H.R.  Rep. No. 103-9, at 16
(1993).  And the Senate report described covered
activities as including “the mailing of list verification
notices or conducting a canvas.”  S. Rep. No. 103-6, at
19 (1993).  None of these reports made any mention of
limiting the 90 -Day Provision to residence -change
sweeps—or, for that matter, any qualification
whatsoever to the statute’s broad language.
And while the NVRA generally was a legislative
“compromise,” U.S. Br. 40, that is not a license to
accept an illogical construction of the statute when a
more coherent one is available.  See Home Depot
U.S.A., Inc. v. Jackson , 587 U.S. 435, 453 (2019)
(Alito, J., dissenting) (rejecting a con struction of a
statute where “respondent does not try to defend its
rationality, suggesting instead that it simply reflects
a legislative compromise”).  Even if the 90 -Day
Provision was itself born of legislative compromise,
that does not explain why Congr ess would have
drafted a separate, broadly worded statutory
subsection (90 -Day Provision) simply to prevent
removals based on changes in residence.  As
demonstrated by Congress’s extremely detailed
procedure for how  to remove an individual on the
basis of a change in residence, see 52 U.S.C.
§ 20507(d), there is no reason to think that Congress
wanted to prevent last -minute systematic residence -
change removals through a highly roundabout
construction of subsection (c)(2).
Second, the United States’ contention —that
Congress wrote a broad provision that, in reality, has
only one narrow application because Congress
foresaw that future legislation “might later expand”
that exception, U.S. Br. 41 —is a hypothetical

46
rationale for which the United States cites no support.
The far more reasonable approach is to take the
exceptions to subsection (c)(2) at face value: Congress
knew how to create compromise carve -outs, and this
Court should not further expand those.  Put another
way, the 90 -Day Provision means what it says: it
broadly covers any  kind of systematic removal,
including removals targeted at any kind of ineligible
voter.
c. Finally, petitioner ’s and the United States’
attempts to contort the 90 -Day Provision to exempt
noncitizenship-based systematic removals  fail even
on their own terms.  Even if “ineligible voters” covered
by the provision are only those voters who underwent
“a change that ma[de] a once-eligible voter ineligible,”
Pet’r Br. 45, that necessarily includes noncitizens who
were denaturalized or who renounced their
citizenship.  See, e.g., 8 U.S.C. §§ 1451, 1481.  In fact,
defendants specifically argued below that H.B. 2243
was necessary in part to identify individuals who had
renounced their citizenship, and they cited statistics
showing that thousands of U.S. citizens renounce
each year, including in Arizona.  See 25-1019
Resp’t.App.24a-25a.  Because H.B. 2243 does not
distinguish between previously -eligible voters and
always-ineligible voters, it  would not  pass muster
even under petitioner’s interpretation of the 90 -Day
Provision.
C. States Retain The Power To Prevent
Noncitizens From Voting
Petitioner and the United States  argue the
decision below is untenable because it is tantamount
to allowing noncitizens to  vote.  That absurd
suggestion finds n o support in the statute.  The

47
parties disagree on a number of points but agree on
this one: noncitizens can—and should —be removed
from voter rolls consistent with the NVRA.
1. As the Ninth Circuit made clear, the “plain
language” of the 90 -Day Provision allows states to
systematically remove suspected noncitizens before
the 90 -day window, and states may “continue any
non-systematic cancellation of registrations within
the 90-day window.”  Pet.App.43a.  If states learn that
specific noncitizens are registered to vote, Section 8
leaves them free to initiate an “investigation” based
on “individualized information.”  Arcia, 772 F.3d at
1344.  So, states continue to have two robust options
to remove suspected noncitizens: (1) systematic
programs or individualized removal more than 90
days before a federal election, or (2) individualized
removal during the 90 days.  See, e.g., Bell v. Marinko,
367 F.3d 588, 591- 92 (6th Cir. 2004).  The NVRA
prohibits only 90-day systematic removals.
States also retain full authority to ensure that only
eligible citizens register to vote in the first place.  The
government fears a “rush of noncitizens” registering
to vote at the eleventh hour.  U.S. Br. 43.  But Section
8 does not prevent states from taking lawful measures
to verify eligibility for individuals registering to vote
at the front end, before they are added to the voter
rolls, whether that happens in the 90 days before a
federal election or not.  Not surprisingly, then, states
have not faced a “rush” of ineligible individ uals—
either noncitizens or sixteen-year-olds—registering to
vote in the final days before an election.  See
Pet.App.227a-229a (unrebutted evidence showing
noncitizen voting in Arizona is exceedingly rare).
2. Notwithstanding the Ninth Circuit’s holding
and respondents’ consistent position, petitioner and

48
the United States suggest that noncitizens could
never be removed unless the Court adopts their
reading.  Specifically, they argue that if noncitizens
qualify as “registrants,” they could never be removed
“because the general removal ban [for registrants in
subsection (a)(3)] also does not expressly exempt
noncitizens.”  U.S. Br. 37; see 52 U.S.C. § 20507(a)(3)
(barring states from removing “the name of a
registrant . . . from the official list of eligible voters”
except under enumerated circumstances).
Respondents agree that  the best reading of the
NVRA is that “registrants” refers to once -“eligible
applicant[s].”  Subsection (a)(1) requires states to
ensure that “any eligible applicant is registered to
vote,” tying applicants who are eligible to vote to the
“regist[ration]” of that applicant to “vote in an
election.”  52 U.S.C. § 20507(a)(1).  So understood,
subsection (a)(3) does not apply to noncitizens, and
adopting respondents’ reading would not prohibi t
states from removing noncitizens altogether.  Such a
reading also respects states’ constitutional authority
to set voting qualifications.  ITCA, 570 U.S. at 16
(“Congress [can] regulate how federal elections are
held, but not who may vote in them.”).
That does not mean that “ineligible voters” and
“eligible voters” must all be “registrants” within the
meaning of the statute.  The NVRA never links the
terms “registrant” and “voter,” nor does it suggest
that “ineligible voters” must all be a subcategory of
previously eligible applicants —a leap that makes
little textual or logical sense for the reasons explained
above.
And the term “registrant” is not subdivided into
“eligible” and “ineligible” subcategories, a textual clue
that Congress thought registrants  are all previously

49
eligible applicants.  By contrast, the NVRA
subdivides “voters” into “eligible” and “ineligible”
subcategories.  That suggests Congress understood
there will be some people on the voter rolls who do not
have the qualifications to vote and others who do, just
as Congress understood there will be some people who
apply to vote who are qualified, and others who are
not.  Nothing about the NVRA’s use of “eligibil[ity]” or
“ineligibil[ity]” suggests that “ineligibility” refers only
to those who were previously eligible.
In the end, all agree: “In creating a list of
justifications for removal, Congress did not intend to
bar the removal of names from the official list of
persons who were ineligible and improperly
registered to vote in the first place.”  Bell, 367 F.3d at
591-92; see also U.S. Student Ass ’n Found. v. Land,
546 F.3d 373, 386 (6th Cir. 2008) (noting that Bell
involved an Ohio state law that removed voters “after
a hearing on the issue” to “determine[] that a
particular challenged individual is not an eligible
voter”) (emphasis omitted).  A ruling in respondents’
favor on the narrow subsection (c)(2) question would
not imply the absurd premise—posited by no party or
court—that the NVRA somehow protects noncitizens
from removal.5

The reading advanced by petitioner and the
United States would destroy Congress’s purposeful
and “hard-fought” choices, U.S. Br. 41, by artificially
narrowing the 90 -Day Provision in ways that are
unsupported by the NVRA’s plain text.  That outcome
would redound to the detriment of eligible citizen
voters.  Congress used capacious terms to give the 90-
Day Provision a broad meaning—not from a mistaken
solicitude for noncitizens, but because it recognized
that “unfair registration laws and procedures can
have a direct and damaging effect on voter
participation in elections ” by citizens .  52 U.S.C.
§ 20501(a)(3).  H.B. 2243 does exactly that.  If
enforced, it would throw election administration into
disarray and risk removing eligible U.S. citizens from
the rolls—with an election looming and only days to
remedy their computer-generated
disenfranchisement.
CONCLUSION
The judgment of the court of appeals should be
affirmed.
